caption:
PostHog published a piece called "Not Everything Needs an LLM." Their point: decision models take a structured question and return a typed answer with a probability, instead of a few hundred words of "it depends."

In their PII pipeline, two narrow yes/no questions decide whether a session summary needs an LLM rewrite. In production, 98.7% skip the LLM call entirely. TechCrunch also reports that in October more than one in four requests on Vercel's AI model router went to decision models, not LLMs.

Here is what I see in companies. The default is to send every task to a generative model. Nobody asks whether generation is needed. And nobody decides which mistake costs more, a false positive or a false negative.

The sources are clear on the limits. A score of 0.85 still means roughly 150 wrong answers per 1,000 checks. Thresholds change between model versions. Multi-step reasoning is still a job for LLMs.

My take: not every problem needs AI, and not every AI problem needs generation. The first production decision is whether you need an LLM at all. If a small model returning a probability over fixed options does the job, it is easier to measure and easier to trust.
